name: HSBC
summary: HSBC's interviews are commonly described as structured and competency-based: interviewers ask about specific occasions when you showed an ability, and why you want HSBC, banking and the business area. The bank publishes four values (we value difference, we succeed together, we take responsibility, we get it done). For graduate and technology programmes, candidates usually report online assessments before an interview or assessment centre.
rounds: Short online application with eligibility questions and, for some roles, a CV
Online assessments of cognitive and behavioural skills; technology programmes add a coding assessment
Video interview for some roles, live or recorded without an interviewer
Interview or assessment centre (a 'Super Day' in the US), often around three hours with exercises and team interviews
For experienced hires, usually a recruiter screen, then one or more interviews of roughly 30–60 minutes with the hiring team
looks_for: A clear reason for choosing HSBC, the industry and the business area
Specific examples: the situation, your task, what you did and the result
Care for customers and for doing things the right way in a regulated business

questions.text: Tell me about a time you looked for a view very different from your own and it changed your approach.
covers: Whose view you sought out and why you thought you needed it
What it showed you that you had missed
What you did differently and how the result changed

questions.text: Describe a time you worked with people in another team, country or time zone to deliver something.
covers: What the work needed from each side
How you handled distance, hand-offs or different ways of working
The result, and what you would set up earlier next time

questions.text: Tell me about a time you owned a mistake before anyone else noticed it.
covers: What went wrong and how you spotted it
Who you told and how quickly
The fix, and the check you added so it didn't happen again

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to move fast and still get the details right.
covers: Why speed mattered and what was at stake if you got it wrong
What you checked carefully and what you decided could wait
The outcome, ideally with a time or error figure

questions.text: Tell me about a time you raised a concern about something that didn't feel right.
covers: What you noticed and why it mattered: a customer, a rule or a risk
How you raised it, and with whom
What happened next and whether you would handle it the same way

questions.text: A customer's international payment hasn't arrived after several days. How would you find out why and explain it to them?
covers: Checks first: the details entered, cut-off times, intermediary banks, compliance holds
Explaining the position plainly, without blaming the customer or guessing
A clear next step, a time to call back, and logging the case

questions.text: What are know-your-customer checks and anti-money-laundering screening, and why do they matter to a global bank?
covers: Verifying who a customer is, what their business does and where their money comes from
Sanctions screening and monitoring transactions for unusual patterns
Why it matters: harm from financial crime, regulatory penalties and loss of trust
Balancing thorough checks with a smooth experience for honest customers

questions.text: How would you design a service that shows customers the status of an international payment as it moves?
covers: Clarifying questions: volume, channels, who can see what
Status events from payment processing into a store the app can read quickly
Handling out-of-order or repeated events, privacy and an audit trail

questions.text: An overnight batch job that posts transactions to accounts failed halfway. How would you handle it?
covers: Impact first: which accounts and customers, and what deadline you face
Re-running safely without posting anything twice, then reconciling
Telling the right people, finding the root cause and preventing a repeat

questions.text: A customer has savings sitting in a current account and asks what to do with them. How would you approach the conversation?
covers: Understanding goals, time horizon, attitude to risk and what they already hold
Recommending only what suits them, with the risks and charges explained
Writing it down and agreeing a follow-up

questions.text: Explain the difference between credit risk and market risk to someone new to banking.
covers: Credit risk: a borrower or counterparty fails to pay
Market risk: losses from moves in interest rates, currencies or prices
An example of each and one way a bank limits it

questions.text: Sign-ups to a bank's mobile app fell sharply in one market last month. How would you find out why?
covers: Checking the data and tracking first
Breaking the drop down by step in the sign-up journey, device and channel
Likely causes, such as a new release, an extra identity check or a campaign ending, and how you'd confirm one

questions.text: Why HSBC, and why this business area?
covers: Something specific about HSBC: its international network, the business or the programme
Why this area fits your skills and interests
What you have done to learn about it

questions.text: Which of HSBC's four values matters most to you, and when have you shown it?
covers: One value, named once
A short example with your own actions and the result
Why that way of working suits you

questions.text: What would you like to ask the team you'd be joining?
covers: A question about the work itself or a current project
How success is judged in the first few months
Something you couldn't have found on the website

tips: Use HSBC's Practice Zone before the online assessments, and take them somewhere quiet without interruptions.
Prepare three 'why' answers: why HSBC, why banking or financial services, and why this business area.
Read the feedback report HSBC emails after the assessments; it shows where you did well and what to work on before the next stage.
For technology programmes, expect a coding assessment even if you didn't study computing; practise explaining your code as you write it.
Know HSBC's purpose, 'Opening up a world of opportunity', and have one example ready for each of the four values.
HSBC's guidance allows AI tools for preparing, such as practising answers, but not for generating responses during live or recorded interviews.
